tour.title: System Overview
tour.description: The CLAUDE.md file is the authoritative developer reference for this project: it explains the full stack (Next.js 16 App Router, Supabase, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui), the three user roles (candidate, institution, admin), the two Supabase client patterns (SSR user session vs. service-role bypass), and the data flow pattern of server-component pages passing props to *-client.tsx interactive components. Reading this first gives you the mental model needed to navigate every other file in the codebase.

tour.title: System Specification
tour.description: The giuus-spec.md documents the full product design: user personas (מועמד/מוסד/מנהל), the complete site map, the data model, role-based access control rules, business logic for the matching/application/invitation workflow, and every API route. This spec is the source of truth for why the code is structured the way it is — understanding the business rules here makes every subsequent API route and page immediately comprehensible.

tour.title: Database Schema
tour.description: The Supabase schema defines the entire data model. The `profiles` table is the root identity record for every user (extending Supabase auth.users with role and phone). From there, `candidates` and `institutions` extend profiles into domain entities. The `jobs`, `applications`, `invitations`, and `interviews` tables form the recruitment pipeline — a candidate applies to a job (applications), an institution invites a candidate (invitations), and an interview is scheduled (interviews). The `notifications` table powers the in-app notification bell.
tour.languageLesson: Supabase uses PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) policies to enforce per-role data access at the database layer. The service-role client bypasses RLS entirely, which is why it is only used in server-side API routes after an explicit role check — never in client components.

tour.title: Shared Types and Constants
tour.description: With the database schema understood, `lib/types.ts` (fanIn=26) translates those tables into TypeScript interfaces — Profile, Candidate, Institution, Job, Application, Notification, Invitation, Interview — used in every component and API route. `lib/constants.ts` (fanIn=10) complements this with domain enumerations: DISTRICTS, JOB_TYPES, SPECIALIZATIONS, INSTITUTION_TYPES, and status label/color maps. Together these two files define the shared vocabulary of the entire system.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript discriminated unions appear throughout types.ts — for example a Role type of 'candidate' | 'institution' | 'admin' lets TypeScript narrow which dashboard component to render at compile time, catching role-routing bugs before runtime.

tour.title: Supabase Clients and Middleware
tour.description: The most-imported file in the entire codebase by a large margin is `lib/supabase/server.ts` (fanIn=98). It exports two factory functions: `createClient()` for cookie-based SSR sessions that respect RLS, and `createServiceClient()` for service-role access that bypasses RLS. The companion `lib/supabase/client.ts` (fanIn=12) provides the browser-side client for client components. The `middleware.ts` file wires these together into Next.js middleware, refreshing sessions on every request and enforcing authentication on all non-public routes.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js middleware (the `middleware.ts` / `proxy.ts` file at the project root) runs on the Edge runtime before every request. It cannot import Node.js modules — which is why the Supabase session refresh logic is isolated in `lib/supabase/middleware.ts` using the SSR-compatible client, and the middleware simply delegates to it.

tour.title: Application Entry and Auth Flow
tour.description: The application starts at `app/layout.tsx`, which sets RTL Hebrew metadata, registers the PWA manifest and service worker, and wraps all pages in a React Query provider. `app/page.tsx` is the public landing page where users choose their role and sign in via Google OAuth. Clicking sign-in triggers `app/auth/callback/route.ts`, which exchanges the OAuth code for a session, looks up or creates the user's profile, and redirects first-time users into the appropriate registration flow. `app/actions.ts` provides the server action for email/password login.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js Server Actions (like `loginAction` in app/actions.ts) run on the server but are called directly from client components, eliminating the need for a dedicated API route for form submissions. They are defined with the `'use server'` directive and can redirect, set cookies, and interact with Supabase directly.

tour.title: Registration Flows by Role
tour.description: Three separate registration paths exist, reflecting the three user roles. Candidates fill a five-step wizard (`app/register/candidate/page.tsx`) collecting personal details, education, experience, and skills, then wait for admin approval tracked in the `candidate_requests` table. Institutions register via the /mosad landing page which calls `app/api/profile/route.ts` to create their institution row and send a pending-approval email. Admins register at `app/register/admin/page.tsx` using a secret code. The OTP verification pages (`app/(auth)/verify-otp/page.tsx`) add a two-factor SMS step for non-admin logins.

tour.title: Dashboard Shell and Role Routing
tour.description: `app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx` (fanOut=8) is the root layout for every authenticated page. It enforces authentication, checks role-based route access using a `canAccess()` function, computes pending badge counts for the sidebar, and renders the header and sidebar shell. The `app/(dashboard)/dashboard/page.tsx` is then the branching point: it prefetches role-specific data from Supabase and renders one of three sub-dashboards — DashboardClient for admins, CandidateDashboard for candidates, or InstitutionDashboard for institutions. This pattern (one server page, three client sub-components) appears throughout the codebase.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js route groups (folders wrapped in parentheses like `(dashboard)`) let you share a layout across many pages without adding that folder segment to the URL. The `app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx` applies to all pages under /dashboard, /jobs, /candidates, etc., while the URL never shows '(dashboard)'.

tour.title: Candidate Journey
tour.description: The candidate experience follows a clear lifecycle: browse jobs in `components/jobs/jobs-client.tsx`, view a job detail at `app/(dashboard)/jobs/[id]/page.tsx` where `apply-button.tsx` handles the application POST, then track applications via `app/(dashboard)/my-applications/page.tsx`. Received interview invitations appear in `app/(dashboard)/my-invitations/my-invitations-client.tsx` where candidates can accept or decline. The profile editing form at `app/(dashboard)/profile/profile-form-client.tsx` (fanOut=12) is the most complex single component — it handles CV upload to Supabase Storage and all candidate field updates.

tour.title: Institution Journey
tour.description: Once an institution is approved by an admin, its staff can post jobs using `components/institution/job-form.tsx` (which supports template saving and loading), view incoming applications in `components/institution/applications-inbox-client.tsx`, and browse the AI-matched candidate recommendations in `app/(dashboard)/institution/matches/matches-client.tsx`. The matches page fetches scored candidate-job pairs from `/api/institution/matches/route.ts` which ranks by district, specialization, and city proximity. Interview scheduling and invitation sending both trigger the notification pipeline.

tour.title: Notification System
tour.description: Every significant event in the system fires through a two-layer notification pipeline. `lib/notify.ts` (fanIn=3) handles in-app notifications: it inserts a row into the `notifications` table and pushes to all browser subscriptions via `lib/webpush.ts`. `lib/notify-external.ts` handles outbound channel routing: it sends WhatsApp if the user prefers it, falls back to SMS, or optionally emails. `lib/email.ts` (fanIn=14, fanOut=19) is the most-imported business logic file — it exports 12 typed async functions covering every email scenario in the recruitment lifecycle via the Resend service.
tour.languageLesson: The pattern `Promise.allSettled([email(), sms(), whatsapp()])` appears in several API routes (e.g., institution approval). Unlike `Promise.all`, `allSettled` never rejects — each notification channel failure is independent, so a failed SMS does not prevent the email from being sent.

tour.title: WhatsApp Chatbot Webhook
tour.description: The WhatsApp chatbot is the system's most architecturally distinctive feature. `app/api/webhooks/whatsapp/route.ts` (fanOut=8) implements a stateful multi-turn conversation engine stored in database session records. The `lib/whatsapp.ts` library (fanIn=6) wraps the Meta Graph API to send messages, parse incoming webhook payloads, and detect Hebrew/English user intent from freeform text using `parseIntent()`. Through this bot, candidates can register, browse jobs, apply, and confirm interviews entirely via WhatsApp — without ever opening a browser.
tour.languageLesson: The WhatsApp webhook implements a state machine pattern using the database as the state store. Each incoming message from a user is looked up against their session record (flow step, collected data so far), the next step is determined, and the session is updated. This makes the multi-turn conversation resumable across server restarts — an important constraint in serverless environments.

tour.title: Automated Cron Jobs
tour.description: Vercel Cron orchestrates seven automated workflows defined in `vercel.json`: daily interview reminders sent 24 hours before scheduled interviews (`app/api/cron/interview-reminders/route.ts`), weekly job alerts matching new postings to candidates (`app/api/cron/job-alerts/route.ts`), automatic expiry of pending invitations after 7 days (`app/api/cron/invitation-reminders/route.ts`), job expiry at their end date (`app/api/cron/job-expiry/route.ts`), reminders to institutions with stale pending applications, and bilateral satisfaction surveys sent 30 days after a placement (`app/api/cron/placement-surveys/route.ts`). Every cron uses the notifications table for idempotent deduplication.
tour.languageLesson: Vercel Cron Jobs are defined in vercel.json as HTTP routes called on a cron schedule. Each route is a standard Next.js API route that receives a GET request. The idempotency pattern used here (checking the notifications table before sending) is critical — Vercel may retry failed cron invocations, so the same reminder must not be sent twice.

tour.title: Admin View and Matching Engine
tour.description: The admin layer sits above all three user journeys. `app/(dashboard)/admin/candidates/page.tsx` provides a searchable, filterable table of all candidates with bulk WhatsApp link generation. `app/(dashboard)/admin/matches/page.tsx` shows AI-matched candidate-job pairs scored by district, specialization, and city proximity from `/api/admin/matches/route.ts`. Admins can approve institutions (`app/api/institutions/[id]/approve/route.ts` fires email+SMS+WhatsApp+in-app simultaneously), manage admin accounts, view the audit log, and export CSV reports.

tour.title: PWA and Configuration
tour.description: `config:package.json` declares all project dependencies — key packages include Supabase SSR, Radix UI/shadcn, Recharts for dashboard charts, web-push for browser push notifications, Resend for email, and Zustand for state. The PWA infrastructure consists of `public/manifest.json` (declaring the app as an installable Hebrew RTL standalone app), `public/sw.js` (cache-first service worker with push notification display), and `components/layout/install-pwa.tsx` (the floating install banner). This makes the entire recruitment system installable as a native-feeling app on both iOS and Android.
tour.languageLesson: Progressive Web Apps use a service worker (sw.js) registered at the root scope to intercept fetch events and serve cached responses when offline. The `beforeinstallprompt` event is captured in app/layout.tsx and deferred, then triggered by the install banner — this is the standard pattern for deferring the browser's native install prompt until the user has engaged with the app.
